Pan American Airways Co.
Manila, Philippine Isis.

Frankly I think you described

if we can hold our position by some tenuous

friends it may be helpful when the day of set-
tlement arrives, but I recall your saying sometime ago that any effort
to cooperate or participate in the operations of CNAC under present
conditions night simply result in our being declared "in" when the
final probable debacle comes, naking it even more difficult for us to
try to revert to a settlement on the basis of the status quo of August
thirteenth. It seems to me that in the end our settlement is very
likely to be arranged through some form of diplomatic claim, and I
doubt whether our chances there would be notably improved by our re-
entry into the picture at this time. However, the President feels that
from the lashington angle it would be a very good thing if we could con-
tinue to hold some sort of à position in China.
He also had in mind the possibility that we might work
out some further financing from the Iport and Export Bank. 1h18 was

have Col. Lun's word for it that Pan American will be made a payment
as soon as the piane reaches Hankow, and I hope your faith will be
justified. I also hope that the sale of the Comsodores will go through
without any further hitch and will be satisfactorily handled at Hong
Kong in your absence.
To close with a light touch, if there can be such a
thing in such a serious situation, I was much intrigued at your state-
ment that it is planned to operate a service from Chungking to Hong
Kong with a DC-2 via Kweiyang and "a point in Kwangsi Province". You
can inagine what Mr. Priester's feelings would be towards such a care-
fully prepared operation as this! Fortunately he does not consider
these operations now to be under his supervision, as I would certeinly
never date to lay this suggestion before him. I find on the map there
are a lot of towns in Kwangsi, and I assume any of them will do for the
purpose you wati have in mind! I am a bit at a loss to know how you
are going to get gasoline and other supplies in there, as well as to
Kreiyang, and the thought of inaugurating this operation over this un-
surveyed route with Mesars. Sweet, Smith, and another whose name you
do not even know, together with the prospect of coning into Canton
(which I understand is periodically under attack by the Japanese air
force) fills me with apprehension. Furthermore, as this is a round-
about route with Eurasia holding
the advantage of the shorter line Canton-
Hankow, I wonder if you really think the operation would be worth the
risks and difficulties involved.
I doubt if we would get much, if any,
international airmail over that route, in which case it would only be
of doubtful political value so far as
the Washington picture is con-
cerned.
Referring above to the Japanese brings up another thought
which I am sure you have not lost sight of, which is the very doubtful
value of any assurances or guarantees you may obtain from the Japanese
The papers only yesterday reported the machine-gunning of
three official automobiles which had the British flag painted on their
roofs. It is true that they were travelling fairly near the scene of
active operations, but of course the Japanese aircraft must cruise
fairly widely. I am wondering, just how much faith you can put in the
green color with which you plan to baptize the CNAC planes. I also re-
call that in one of your earlier letters you put the danger to our
planes as being from the Chinese and Japanese militaries in that order.
In concluding this rather gloomy letter, which I hope
wil1 not arrive until everything has been worked out right, let
in all sincerity that I admire very much your even trying to go ahead
on these plans, and the desperate efforts you are making to work out
something to protect the conpany's interests.
I only hope that you will
not let your anxiety to achieve the impossible lead you too far.

Mr. Bixby
- 4 -
October 15, 1957
I assume I will not hear from you for some time, and
